title: The Coding Interview Format
summary: What a coding round actually evaluates and how its shape shifts by stage and company, so prep effort targets the real rubric instead of a guess.

slides.markdown:
A coding interview looks like a puzzle. It is actually a **structured evaluation with a rubric you never see**, run inside a fixed time box by someone who has done this dozens of times this quarter.

Most prep effort goes into solving problems. That matters, but it is only one of four things being scored, and candidates who don't know the other three routinely lose to candidates who wrote worse code.

This topic maps the format itself — what's measured, who's in the room, and how the shape changes across phone screen, onsite, and company size — so the rest of this group's advice lands on solid ground.

slides.subTitle: "Did it run" is one signal out of four
slides.markdown:
Every coding round scores four things, whether or not the interviewer says so out loud:

- **Correctness** — does it handle the stated problem and the edge cases you'd expect a careful engineer to catch?
- **Communication** — can the interviewer follow your thinking well enough to write a coherent debrief afterward?
- **Complexity** — do you know the cost of what you built, and can you improve it when asked?
- **Code quality** — names, structure, and whether a teammate could read this six months from now.

A candidate who nails correctness and complexity but works in total silence often scores *lower* than one who talks through a slightly rougher solution — because the first produces no evidence for the debrief beyond "the code worked," and that alone rarely clears the bar.

The four dimensions aren't weighted equally, and the weighting shifts with seniority:

| Dimension | Junior/new-grad | Senior+ |
|---|---|---|
| Correctness | High — a wrong answer is hard to recover from | Expected, less discussed |
| Communication | Moderate | High — this *is* the signal at senior level |
| Complexity | Moderate | High, including trade-offs, not just the number |
| Code quality | Moderate | Moderate-high, judged against production habits |

At junior level, a working solution said quietly can still pass. At senior level, the same silent-but-correct solution reads as a red flag: staff engineers are hired partly to explain decisions to other people, and a round with no narration gives no evidence of that.

slides.sectionTitle: Phone screen vs onsite vs virtual-onsite
slides.markdown:
| Stage | Length | Problems | Stakes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Phone screen | 30–45 min | 1, sometimes 2 short | Pass/fail gate to the loop |
| Virtual onsite | 45–60 min per round, several rounds | 1–2 per round | Each round scored independently |
| In-person onsite | Same as virtual, plus breaks and a host | 1–2 per round | Same, plus informal signal from breaks/lunch |

The phone screen is deliberately shorter and shallower — it exists to filter out candidates who can't code at all, not to probe depth. Treating it like a full onsite round (over-explaining, over-optimizing) burns time you don't have. Save the depth for the loop you're screening into.

A well-run round has a predictable rhythm, and knowing it lets you pace yourself instead of guessing how much time is left for what.

Roughly: 2–3 minutes of small talk and problem reveal, 3–5 minutes of clarifying questions, 5–10 minutes reaching an approach, 15–20 minutes coding, 5–10 minutes testing and refining, and a few minutes at the end for your questions back.

The biggest time sink for underprepared candidates is spending 20 of the 45 minutes just getting to a stated approach — which leaves almost no time to code, let alone test.

slides.sectionTitle: Who's in the room, and what happens after
slides.markdown:
Usually it's one interviewer, sometimes a silent shadow being trained. What matters more than the room is what happens **after** you leave it.

The interviewer writes a debrief — a short written scorecard against the rubric in §2, with specific evidence, not just a number. That debrief, not their memory of you, is what a hiring committee reads days or weeks later. If you didn't say something out loud, it usually isn't in the debrief, even if you clearly thought it.

This is the practical reason narration matters: your reasoning only counts toward the decision if it left a trace the interviewer could write down.

slides.sectionTitle: FAANG-style loop vs startup single round
slides.markdown:
| | Large-company loop | Startup single round |
|---|---|---|
| Structure | 4–6 independent rounds, separate interviewers | 1–2 rounds, sometimes the same person twice |
| Scoring | Each round scored alone, then averaged/committee | Often one holistic judgment |
| Recovery from one bad round | Possible — other rounds can outweigh it | Much harder — it may be the whole signal |
| Calibration | Interviewers trained on a shared rubric | Rubric is often informal, interviewer-specific |

The practical takeaway: in a large loop, one rough round is recoverable, so don't spiral if you stumble in round two of five. In a startup's single round, treat every minute as load-bearing — there's no later round to make up ground.

slides.sectionTitle: How many problems, and how hard
slides.markdown:
Most rounds run **one problem with follow-ups**, not several unrelated problems. The follow-up is usually one of: tighten the complexity, handle a new constraint ("now the input is a stream"), or scale the design ("now there are a billion rows").

Difficulty typically starts at a level you should solve within the time box, then escalates only if you finish early — the escalation isn't a trap, it's the interviewer running out of runway on the first problem and wanting more signal. Panicking when a follow-up appears ("I thought I was done") reads as a lack of familiarity with the format itself, not as a knowledge gap.

slides.sectionTitle: Solving it correctly and still failing
slides.markdown:
The single most confusing outcome for candidates: a working, correct solution that still gets a **no**.

It happens when the debrief has no evidence for the other three rubric dimensions — the candidate coded in silence, never stated a complexity, or needed three hints to get unstuck without saying so. From the interviewer's side, a silent correct solution and a *memorized* correct solution look identical on paper; the debrief can't distinguish "this person can reason" from "this person has seen this exact problem before."

The fix isn't more LeetCode. It's producing evidence for correctness, communication, complexity, *and* quality inside the same round — which the rest of this group builds skill for.

slides.sectionTitle: What a staff-level round looks for differently
slides.markdown:
At staff level, interviewers often skip straight to a harder problem or add architectural follow-ups ("how would this run across multiple machines") because raw problem-solving is assumed, not tested.

What they're actually probing: does this person **question the problem itself** — pushing back on a premise, proposing a different framing — rather than accepting it at face value? Does their code read like something they'd actually ship, with the boring parts (error handling, naming) intact under time pressure? A staff candidate who treats the round as "solve this LeetCode problem fast" under-performs a senior candidate who treats it as "demonstrate how I'd operate on a real problem with a clock running."

Knowing the format is the floor. The rest of this group turns each rubric dimension into a practiced skill: asking the right [clarifying questions](clarifying-coding-requirements) before you code, [narrating your thinking](narrating-your-approach) as you go, recognizing which [pattern](pattern-recognition) a problem is signaling, and [talking through complexity](complexity-communication) without fumbling it.

For the algorithms and data structures those patterns draw on, this area deliberately doesn't re-teach them — that's the job of the `data-structures-algorithms` area. This group is about the performance layer sitting on top of technical knowledge you build there.
